flashcards.q: What are xmin and xmax, and what's the Postgres tuple visibility rule?
flashcards.a: xmin = transaction ID that created the tuple version, xmax = transaction ID that deleted/superseded it (0/unset = live). Visible to a snapshot if xmin's txn committed before the snapshot AND (xmax unset OR xmax's txn hasn't committed as of the snapshot).

flashcards.q: When is a Postgres transaction's snapshot taken, per isolation level?
flashcards.a: Read Committed: a fresh snapshot at the start of EVERY statement (so two SELECTs in one transaction can see different data - read skew possible). Repeatable Read / Serializable: ONE snapshot at transaction start, reused for the whole transaction.

2PL: shared lock on read, exclusive on write, held until commit; readers block writers and vice versa; needs predicate locks (not just row locks) to stop phantoms. MVCC: readers see an older committed version instead of waiting, so readers never block writers or vice versa - at the cost of write-write conflicts needing detection (first-committer-wins) and write skew slipping through.

flashcards.q: Define all six anomalies in one line each.
flashcards.a: Dirty read: see another txn's uncommitted write. Dirty write: overwrite another txn's uncommitted write. Read skew: same row read twice in one txn, different committed values. Phantom read: predicate query's result set changes mid-txn. Lost update: same row read-modify-write, one write clobbers the other. Write skew: DIFFERENT rows, disjoint writes jointly violate an invariant neither write alone broke.

flashcards.q: The doctors-on-call write skew repro, in one sentence.
flashcards.a: Invariant: at least 1 doctor on call. Alice and Bob both on call; each reads count=2 from their own snapshot, each independently concludes it's safe to go off-call, each updates only their own row, both commit -> final count = 0, invariant violated, no write-write conflict ever detected.

flashcards.q: Why does snapshot isolation prevent read skew but NOT write skew?
flashcards.a: Read skew is prevented directly by the fixed snapshot (repeated reads see one consistent point in time). Write skew isn't about the snapshot changing - it's about an invariant relating two transactions' independent decisions, violated by writes to DIFFERENT rows, which SI's same-row conflict detection never checks.

flashcards.q: Level -> anomalies permitted, memorize the table.
flashcards.a: Read Uncommitted: all possible except dirty write. Read Committed: dirty read/write prevented, rest possible. Repeatable Read (ANSI min): + read skew prevented. Snapshot Isolation (Postgres REPEATABLE READ): + phantom + lost update prevented; WRITE SKEW STILL POSSIBLE. Serializable: everything prevented.

flashcards.q: Real default isolation level per database.
flashcards.a: Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server -> READ COMMITTED. MySQL/InnoDB -> REPEATABLE READ (with gap locks that suppress most phantoms beyond the ANSI minimum).

Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is implemented as snapshot isolation, not true serializability - no SSI, no 2PL predicate locking at that level. Write skew is still possible on Oracle SERIALIZABLE despite the name.

flashcards.q: How does Postgres's SSI detect write skew without blocking readers?
flashcards.a: SERIALIZABLE transactions take SIREAD locks on data they read - bookkeeping only, never blocking. A later write to SIREAD-covered data creates an rw-antidependency edge. If edges form a cycle through a pivot transaction (incoming + outgoing rw-antidependency to concurrent transactions), Postgres aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, forcing a retry.

flashcards.q: Two fixes for write skew besides full SERIALIZABLE, and when each wins.
flashcards.a: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the invariant-backing rows - targeted, cheap, but requires correctly enumerating every dangerous read. Atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE cond (e.g. seats_available > 0) - best for simple capacity checks, folds check-then-write into one atomic statement, avoids held-lock time and retry loops.

flashcards.q: Lost update vs write skew - the key structural difference.
flashcards.a: Lost update: SAME row read by both, one write overwrites the other, an update is literally lost. Write skew: DIFFERENT rows written, no write is lost or overwritten - the invariant relating the two rows is the casualty, not any single value.

flashcards.q: Why does snapshot isolation prevent lost update in Postgres specifically?
flashcards.a: First-committer-wins: the second transaction's write to the SAME row triggers a serialization failure (must retry) rather than silently overwriting. This is a real protection SI provides - it's write skew (disjoint rows) that survives, not same-row lost update.

flashcards.q: What does XID wraparound risk mean operationally?
flashcards.a: Postgres XIDs are 32-bit, wrapping every ~4 billion transactions. Autovacuum's 'freeze' rewrites old tuples' xmin to a frozen sentinel to prevent ambiguity. An under-vacuumed high-write table risks Postgres forcing itself into read-only mode to prevent corruption as the counter approaches wraparound.

flashcards.q: Why do predicate locks matter for 2PL, and what happens without them?
flashcards.a: Row locks alone only stop conflicts on rows that already existed when the lock was taken - they don't stop phantoms. Predicate locks lock the range/condition a query scanned, so a NEW row inserted into that range is caught too; without them, phantom reads slip through even under strict 2PL.
